quote: The medication change in the last 72 hours names the syndrome — always reconstruct it.
problem: The pearl makes a medication change in the last 72 h the defining clue. NMS often starts days to weeks into treatment and can occur on a stable dose, especially with dehydration, heat, agitation or IM loading. Malignant catatonia may have no drug trigger at all.
whyItMatters: A learner who finds no recent medication change in a rigid, febrile patient who has been on a stable antipsychotic for weeks may push NMS down the list and delay stopping the drug.
evidence: Strawn, Keck & Caroff, Am J Psychiatry 2007 (the page's own cited source): most NMS cases begin within the first days to weeks of treatment, but NMS can occur at any point during antipsychotic exposure, and dehydration and agitation are risk factors.
correction: The medication history — especially changes in the last 72 hours, though NMS can arise after weeks on a stable dose — usually names the syndrome; always reconstruct it.

quote: When a patient makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the **duty to protect (Tarasoff)** is triggered; escalate to your supervising clinician immediately rather than deciding alone.
problem: The page presents the duty to protect as a universal trigger. US states differ: some mandate a duty to warn or protect, some permit disclosure without requiring it, and a few have no statutory duty. They also differ on what threat triggers the duty and what discharges it. The linked violence.html tool says obligations vary by state; this page does not.
whyItMatters: Learners in other states would absorb the wrong legal rule, which matters if the curriculum is adopted nationally. Escalating to a supervisor is correct everywhere; the stated legal trigger is not.
evidence: State duty-to-warn/protect statutes vary (e.g., the NCSL 'Mental Health Professionals' Duty to Warn' survey: mandatory, permissive, or no duty). The page's own violence.html tool says 'Duty-to-protect obligations vary by state'.
correction: When a patient makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, a **duty to protect (Tarasoff)** may be triggered — whether it is mandatory, permissive, or absent, and what discharges it, varies by state; escalate to your supervising clinician immediately rather than deciding alone.

verification.reason: In violence.md's Management paragraph the duty is stated as 'is triggered' with no state qualifier. The 'vary by state' caveat appears only in the separate FRST tool text (line ~681), not on this page. The correction adds the variation and keeps the escalation instruction.
verification.evidence: recall: NCSL survey of mental health professionals' duty to warn (mandatory / permissive / none by state); page's own FRST tool text 'Duty-to-protect obligations vary by state'.

quote: for buprenorphine, generally wait for COWS ≥8–12 to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
problem: There is no fentanyl caveat. With high-potency synthetic opioids, precipitated withdrawal can occur even at these scores, and ASAM 2023 adds high-dose and low-dose initiation strategies.
whyItMatters: In a fentanyl-dominant drug supply, a learner who treats COWS 8–12 as a safe threshold may help set up a precipitated withdrawal. That drives treatment dropout and return to use, with overdose risk.
evidence: ASAM Clinical Considerations: Buprenorphine Treatment of OUD for Individuals Using High-potency Synthetic Opioids, J Addict Med 2023 (doi:10.1097/ADM.0000000000001202). The exact recommended threshold is not verified here; the guidance's existence and scope are.
correction: for buprenorphine, generally wait for COWS ≥8–12 to avoid precipitated withdrawal; with fentanyl use, precipitated withdrawal can still occur — follow your protocol, which may use a high-dose or low-dose initiation strategy.
verified: WebSearch confirmed the ASAM 2023 HPSO clinical-considerations document exists; specific COWS threshold not confirmed

verification.reason: The tool string carries no fentanyl caveat. ASAM 2023 HPSO Table 3 pairs COWS ≥8 with an objective sign with standard or high-dose initiation, and COWS <8 with standard or low-dose initiation. It does not describe a higher COWS threshold, so the reviewer's 'higher threshold' wording is unsupported. I reworded the correction to the strategies ASAM actually names.
verification.evidence: ASAM Clinical Considerations: Buprenorphine Treatment of OUD for Individuals Using High-potency Synthetic Opioids, J Addict Med 2023, doi:10.1097/ADM.0000000000001202 (ASAM-hosted PDF, Table 3)

quote: {t:"24–48 h",h:"Withdrawal seizures"
problem: The timeline puts alcohol-withdrawal seizures at 24–48 h. They typically occur 6–48 h after the last drink and peak around 12–24 h, often before hallucinosis or DTs.
whyItMatters: A learner reading the timeline would think seizure risk starts at 24 h. They might under-treat, or not anticipate a seizure, in a patient 8–20 h from the last drink, which is exactly the window when most present to a unit.
evidence: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020), Table/clinical course: seizures can occur 6–48 h after cessation. Standard texts (Kaplan & Sadock) give a peak at about 12–24 h.
correction: {t:"6–48 h (peak ~12–24 h)",h:"Withdrawal seizures"

verification.reason: Alcohol-withdrawal seizures cluster 6–48 h after the last drink, with a peak around 12–24 h (Victor & Adams' classic series; ASAM 2020 clinical-course description). A timeline entry starting at 24 h misplaces the peak risk window. Coordinator note: the 24–48 h figure matches the First Aid for USMLE table that students study from, so faculty may want to acknowledge that discrepancy. The correction fits the {t:...} string.
verification.evidence: Recall: Victor M, Adams RD 1953 (seizures largely 7–48 h, peak 13–24 h); ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management 2020 (https://www.asam.org/quality-care/clinical-guidelines/alcohol-withdrawal-management-guideline).

quote: Hold benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants pre-ECT (they blunt the seizure)
problem: This is an unqualified instruction to hold anticonvulsants and benzodiazepines. Anticonvulsants prescribed for epilepsy are continued through ECT. In catatonia, lorazepam is commonly continued alongside ECT: the pre-treatment dose is minimised or timed, or reversed with flumazenil, rather than stopped. The page prose says 'hold/adjust'.
whyItMatters: A learner applying this card could stop an antiepileptic in a patient with epilepsy, risking breakthrough or status seizures. They could also abruptly stop lorazepam in a catatonic patient, risking withdrawal and catatonic relapse.
evidence: APA Task Force on ECT, The Practice of ECT (2nd ed., 2001), §8 (concurrent medications: anticonvulsants continued when prescribed for seizure disorder). Fink & Taylor, catatonia management (combined lorazepam and ECT, with flumazenil as needed).
correction: Minimise or time benzodiazepines and mood-stabilising anticonvulsants pre-ECT (they blunt the seizure) — continue antiepileptics prescribed for epilepsy, and don't abruptly stop lorazepam in catatonia

verification.reason: The overlay key point says 'Hold' without qualification, while the body says 'hold/adjust'. Antiepileptics given for epilepsy are continued through ECT (APA Task Force), and in catatonia lorazepam is minimised or timed (flumazenil if needed) rather than stopped. The correction reads grammatically with the retained clause ', and plan continuation treatment…'.
verification.evidence: recall (APA Task Force on ECT, The Practice of ECT 2nd ed. 2001, concurrent medications; Fink & Taylor catatonia literature)

quote: ketamine/esketamine act within hours on depressive symptoms — not on suicidality itself
problem: For intranasal esketamine the label does say an effect on suicidality has not been demonstrated. For IV ketamine, randomised and individual-participant meta-analytic data do show a rapid reduction in suicidal ideation. The card flatly asserts no effect for both.
whyItMatters: The learner comes away with a false belief about IV ketamine. The page's safety message (it does not replace monitoring or safety planning) holds without the overstatement.
evidence: Wilkinson et al., Am J Psychiatry 2018 (IPD meta-analysis, 10 trials: IV ketamine reduced suicidal ideation within 24 h). Grunebaum et al., Am J Psychiatry 2018 (ketamine vs midazolam, SSI primary outcome positive). Spravato USPI, Limitations of Use.
correction: ketamine/esketamine act within hours on depressive symptoms — any effect on suicidal ideation is short-lived and, for esketamine, not demonstrated

quote: active suicidality, refusal to eat or drink, pregnancy where medications are undesirable, or prior good ECT response
problem: The Indications paragraph lists pregnancy as a stand-alone rapid-response trigger. The overlay and the 'What the student does' list on the same page say pregnancy is not a separate trigger but changes the calculus once an indication is present.
whyItMatters: This is an internal contradiction: a learner could take pregnancy alone as an ECT indication.
evidence: Internal consistency: see this page's overlay key point and 'What the student does' bullet.
correction: active suicidality, refusal to eat or drink, or prior good ECT response (pregnancy makes ECT preferred over drugs once one of these is present)

quote: - **Deep brain stimulation (DBS)** — investigational for refractory depression and OCD.
problem: DBS for severe, treatment-refractory OCD has been FDA-authorised since 2009 under a Humanitarian Device Exemption (Medtronic Reclaim). It is investigational only for depression.
whyItMatters: The learner would believe no neuromodulation device is authorised for refractory OCD beyond TMS.
evidence: FDA HDE H050003 (Reclaim DBS Therapy for OCD), approved February 2009.
correction: - **Deep brain stimulation (DBS)** — investigational for refractory depression; available for severe treatment-refractory OCD under an FDA Humanitarian Device Exemption (2009).

quote: - Hold benzodiazepines/anticonvulsants before ECT (they blunt the seizure).
problem: The pearl repeats the unqualified 'hold' instruction and contradicts the body's own 'hold/adjust'. Antiepileptics for epilepsy are continued, and lorazepam in catatonia is minimised or timed rather than stopped.
whyItMatters: Pearls are memorised verbatim. Stopping an antiepileptic, or stopping lorazepam abruptly in catatonia, can cause seizures or a catatonic relapse.
evidence: APA Task Force on ECT (2001), concurrent medications.
correction: - Minimise or time benzodiazepines and mood-stabilising anticonvulsants before ECT (they blunt the seizure) — but continue antiepileptics given for epilepsy.

verification.reason: Same defect as M06-005, in the pearl, and it contradicts the body's own 'hold/adjust'. The correction is accurate. The lorazepam-in-catatonia caveat is left to the key point, which is acceptable.
verification.evidence: recall (APA Task Force on ECT 2001, concurrent medications)

quote: - Duty to protect (Tarasoff): a serious threat to a reasonably identifiable person overrides confidentiality — warn, notify police, or hospitalize.
problem: The standalone card states the duty to protect as universal. It varies by state: mandatory in some states, permissive in others, and in a few (e.g., Texas, per Thapar v. Zezulka 1999) there is no duty to warn at all, with disclosure limited to what the statute permits. The page prose's 'specifics vary by state' does not appear on the card.
whyItMatters: A learner nationally could believe warning the victim is always required or always permitted. In some states, a warning outside the statute's terms is an unprotected breach, and in others the options that satisfy the duty are specifically listed.
evidence: Tarasoff v. Regents (Cal. 1976). Thapar v. Zezulka, 994 S.W.2d 635 (Tex. 1999). NCSL duty-to-warn state survey (mandatory / permissive / no statute). HIPAA 45 CFR 164.512(j) permits, but does not require, disclosure.
correction: - Duty to protect (Tarasoff): a serious threat to a reasonably identifiable person can override confidentiality: warn, notify police, or hospitalize. Whether this is mandatory, permissive, or absent depends on your state's statute.

verification.reason: The Key-points card states the duty as universal. The page prose hedges ('Specifics vary by state (some mandate warning, some permit it)'), but the overlay card renders on its own above the prose. State law is mandatory, permissive or absent; Texas has no common-law duty to warn (Thapar v. Zezulka). The correction is minimal, accurate and grammatical.
verification.evidence: Tarasoff v. Regents, 17 Cal.3d 425 (1976); Thapar v. Zezulka, 994 S.W.2d 635 (Tex. 1999); NCSL duty-to-warn survey; 45 CFR 164.512(j) (recall for case law).

quote: - Child and elder abuse are mandated reports on reasonable suspicion, not proof; good-faith reporters are protected.
problem: Child-abuse reporting is mandatory for physicians in every state, but elder-abuse reporting is not uniform. At least one large state (New York) has no general mandatory elder-abuse reporting duty for physicians outside care facilities, and reportable categories and reporter lists differ.
whyItMatters: A learner would treat elder-abuse reporting as a universal physician mandate. In some states they would report without the patient's consent when the law makes reporting voluntary and consent-sensitive, and in others they would miss the specific reportable categories.
evidence: State adult-protective-services statutes vary (e.g., NY Social Services Law: reporting of community elder abuse is voluntary for physicians; mandatory only for residents of residential health care facilities under Public Health Law §2803-d). CAPTA-derived child-abuse reporting is mandatory in all states.

The page's own prose on mandatory reporting is not hedged for elder abuse either, so nothing nearby rescues the card. The correction is accurate and drop-in.

quote: the constitutionally required standard of proof is **"clear and convincing evidence"**
problem: Addington v. Texas set clear and convincing evidence as the constitutional minimum. States may, and some do, require proof beyond a reasonable doubt for civil commitment.
whyItMatters: The learner will take clear and convincing evidence to be the standard everywhere, when it is only the floor.
evidence: Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979): due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence, and states are free to adopt a higher standard.
correction: the constitutionally required minimum standard of proof is **"clear and convincing evidence"** (some states require more)

quote: - Child and elder abuse are mandated reports on *reasonable suspicion*; good-faith reporters are protected.
problem: The pearl repeats elder-abuse reporting as a universal mandate. Physician elder-abuse reporting duties vary by state and are voluntary in some (e.g., New York outside care facilities).
whyItMatters: Pearls are memorised as universal rules, so a learner in a voluntary-reporting state would believe they must report.
evidence: State APS statutes vary; NY Public Health Law §2803-d is limited to residential facilities.
correction: - Child abuse is a mandated report on *reasonable suspicion*; elder/dependent-adult abuse is mandated in most states (check yours); good-faith reporters are protected.

verification.reason: This is the same defect in the page's High-yield pearls, and the surrounding prose does not hedge elder-abuse reporting. New York's lack of a general physician mandate is verified. The correction matches M06-009 and is drop-in.

quote: Check a clozapine level about a week after the change — and tell the prescriber it happened.
problem: For smoking cessation (including enforced abstinence on admission) the card's one action is to wait about a week for a level. Clozapine levels rise substantially within days once CYP1A2 induction wears off, and standard guidance is to reduce the dose ahead of the rise, not to wait for a level.
whyItMatters: A learner who follows the card as written tells the prescriber after the fact and waits a week. In that week a newly admitted non-smoking patient can develop clozapine toxicity (sedation, hypotension, seizures) that the card itself warns about.
evidence: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (14th ed., 2021), smoking and psychotropics: on stopping smoking, reduce clozapine dose gradually (roughly 25–50% over about a week) and monitor plasma levels. CYP1A2 de-induction is largely complete within about 1 week. Hiemke et al., AGNP TDM consensus 2017 (cited on the card).
correction: Tell the prescriber the same day — a pre-emptive clozapine dose reduction is usually needed when smoking stops — and check a clozapine level about a week after the change.

verification.reason: The card's single action for a CYP1A2 change, stopping smoking included, is to check a level in about a week and tell the prescriber 'it happened'. It never says a pre-emptive dose reduction is needed. The toxicity signs further down the card are reactive. Standard guidance on stopping smoking is to lower the clozapine dose over about a week and to check levels, and the correction adds that with no dose literal.
verification.evidence: recall: Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 14th ed. (smoking and psychotropics: reduce clozapine gradually toward about 75% of the dose over about a week after stopping, and repeat the level at 1 week); CYP1A2 de-induction is largely complete in about 1 week. Hiemke et al. AGNP TDM consensus 2017.

quote: carbamazepine needs CBC/LFTs/sodium, HLA-B*1502 in at-risk ancestry, and watch for SIADH.
problem: The key-point card calls valproate and lithium teratogens needing β-hCG, then lists carbamazepine's monitoring without saying it is also a teratogen or that it induces contraceptive metabolism.
whyItMatters: Set beside the valproate/lithium sentence, the card implies carbamazepine is a pregnancy-safer alternative that needs no pregnancy test.
evidence: Carbamazepine USPI, Warnings (pregnancy: neural-tube defects) and Drug Interactions (hormonal contraceptives).
correction: carbamazepine is also a teratogen that lowers hormonal-contraceptive levels (β-hCG, contraception counselling) and needs CBC/LFTs/sodium, HLA-B*1502 in at-risk ancestry, and watch for SIADH.

verification.reason: In the key-point bullet, carbamazepine sits right after 'Valproate and lithium are teratogens — β-hCG', which invites the reading that it is the pregnancy-safe option. The page's pearls repeat the same omission. The correction stays grammatical after the semicolon.
verification.evidence: recall: carbamazepine USPI, Warnings (pregnancy) and Drug Interactions (hormonal contraceptives).

quote: **myocarditis (early — check troponin/CRP if symptomatic)**
problem: Troponin/CRP is tied to symptoms only. Clozapine myocarditis clusters in weeks 1–4 and often presents with non-specific findings (fever, tachycardia, malaise) that are easily read as benign early side effects. Widely used protocols check troponin and CRP at baseline and weekly for the first 4 weeks.
whyItMatters: A learner would not order baseline or surveillance troponin/CRP during initiation. They could also put down early tachycardia and fever to 'expected' clozapine effects and miss the leading early cause of death on clozapine, which the same page calls 'the early killer'.
evidence: Ronaldson et al., Aust N Z J Psychiatry 2011 monitoring protocol (baseline plus weekly troponin/CRP for 4 weeks). Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines 14th ed. Clozapine USPI Warnings 5.x (myocarditis is most frequent in the first 2 months). The US label does not mandate routine troponin.
correction: **myocarditis (early, mostly weeks 1–4 — many protocols check troponin/CRP at baseline and weekly for the first 4 weeks; check urgently with fever, tachycardia, chest pain, or flu-like illness)**

verification.reason: The cell ties troponin/CRP to symptoms only, yet the same page calls myocarditis 'the early killer'. Early myocarditis often presents with non-specific fever or tachycardia. US health systems have adopted the Ronaldson baseline-plus-weekly-for-4-weeks protocol. The correction says 'many protocols' rather than asserting a label mandate, which is accurate, because the US label mandates no routine troponin.
verification.evidence: PubMed PMID 31684809 (McNutt et al., J Pharm Pract 2021; doi:10.1177/0897190019882878: a US health-system protocol based on Ronaldson 2011, with troponin and hsCRP at baseline then weekly for 4 weeks); clozapine USPI (myocarditis most frequent in the first 2 months).

quote: | **Carbamazepine** | CBC, LFTs, sodium, level; HLA-B*1502 in at-risk ancestry | Level, CBC, LFTs, sodium | Agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia; SIADH (hyponatremia); Stevens-Johnson (HLA-B*1502); auto-induction of its own metabolism |
problem: The carbamazepine row leaves out that it is a teratogen (neural-tube defects), so there is no β-hCG at baseline. It also leaves out that it is a potent CYP3A4/pan-inducer that lowers hormonal-contraceptive and many psychotropic levels. The valproate and lithium rows both carry pregnancy content.
whyItMatters: The page teaches 'β-hCG before starting' for valproate and lithium only. A learner would start carbamazepine without a pregnancy test or contraception counselling, and would miss that it can make an oral contraceptive fail and drop co-prescribed antipsychotic levels.
evidence: Carbamazepine (Tegretol) USPI, Warnings: Usage in Pregnancy (neural-tube defects) and Drug Interactions (CYP3A4 induction; hormonal contraceptives). CANMAT/ISBD 2018 bipolar guideline, safety monitoring table.
correction: | **Carbamazepine** | CBC, LFTs, sodium, level, β-hCG; HLA-B*1502 in at-risk ancestry | Level, CBC, LFTs, sodium | Agranulocytosis/aplastic anemia; SIADH (hyponatremia); Stevens-Johnson (HLA-B*1502); auto-induction of its own metabolism; potent enzyme inducer (lowers hormonal contraceptives and many psychotropics); teratogen (neural-tube) |

verification.reason: I read the whole table. The valproate and lithium rows carry teratogen/β-hCG content, and the carbamazepine row has none, with no mention of enzyme induction either. Carbamazepine's neural-tube teratogenicity and its lowering of hormonal-contraceptive levels are settled label facts. The correction is a drop-in row replacement.
verification.evidence: recall: carbamazepine USPI, Warnings (Usage in Pregnancy: spina bifida/neural-tube defects) and Drug Interactions (CYP3A4 induction; hormonal contraceptives may be less effective).

quote: - Clozapine initiation requires mandatory ANC monitoring per the hematologic schedule
problem: 'Mandatory' reflects the retired REMS framing. ANC monitoring now continues per the prescribing information and is no longer REMS-enforced, which the page body itself states.
whyItMatters: This is an overlay-vs-prose conflict on current regulation. The learner believes a dispensing requirement still exists.
evidence: FDA DSC on clozapine REMS removal (effective 2025-06-13).
correction: - Clozapine initiation requires ANC monitoring per the prescribing-information schedule (REMS eliminated 2025)
verified: WebFetch of FDA Drug Safety Communication on clozapine REMS removal

quote: requires mandatory ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis
problem: Since the FDA eliminated the clozapine REMS (effective 2025-06-13), ANC monitoring is a prescribing-information recommendation: prescribers 'should continue to monitor ANC' per the PI. It is no longer a mandatory, dispensing-gated requirement. The page prose states this correctly.
whyItMatters: A learner would believe ANC reporting still gates dispensing, which misstates current regulation. The clinical behaviour (monitor ANC) stays correct.
evidence: FDA Drug Safety Communication, 'FDA removes REMS program for clozapine' (REMS removed 2025-06-13; DSC 2025-08-27): 'prescribers should continue to monitor patients' ANC according to the monitoring frequencies described in the prescribing information.'
correction: requires ANC monitoring for agranulocytosis per its prescribing information (the REMS was eliminated in 2025)

quote: roughly one extra case of suicidal ideation/behavior per ~110 treated, against a number-needed-to-treat near 10 for response
problem: The NNH and NNT are given with no study identity. They come from pediatric trials (Bridge et al., JAMA 2007: MDD NNH ≈112, NNT ≈10), yet the sentence attaches them to the 'through age 24' warning.
whyItMatters: Learners cannot trace the figure and may apply pediatric numbers to young adults.
evidence: Bridge JA et al., JAMA 2007;297:1683–96 (pediatric antidepressant RCTs).
correction: roughly one extra case of suicidal ideation/behavior per ~110 treated, against a number-needed-to-treat near 10 for response (pediatric MDD trials; Bridge et al., JAMA 2007)

quote: Xanomeline-Trospium: The First Non-Dopaminergic Antipsychotic
problem: Pimavanserin, a non-dopaminergic 5-HT2A inverse agonist, was FDA-approved in 2016 for Parkinson's disease psychosis. Xanomeline–trospium (2024) is the first antipsychotic for schizophrenia without direct D2 blockade (muscarinic).
whyItMatters: This is a board-style fact taught incorrectly.
evidence: Nuplazid (pimavanserin) FDA approval April 2016. Cobenfy (xanomeline–trospium) FDA approval September 2024.
correction: Xanomeline-Trospium: The First Non-D2-Blocking (Muscarinic) Antipsychotic for Schizophrenia

quote: **Exposure and response prevention (ERP)**, a CBT variant, is the specific evidence-based treatment for OCD and phobias.
problem: ERP is the OCD-specific protocol, because response prevention targets compulsions. Specific phobia is treated with exposure therapy (in vivo exposure or systematic desensitisation), not ERP.
whyItMatters: On the shelf, the answer for specific phobia is exposure therapy or systematic desensitisation, so the conflation invites a wrong-term answer.
evidence: APA OCD practice guideline (2007, watch 2013): ERP. Exposure-based CBT is first-line for specific phobia (DSM-5-TR treatment texts; NICE).
correction: **Exposure and response prevention (ERP)**, a CBT variant, is the specific evidence-based treatment for OCD; exposure therapy is the treatment for phobias.

quote: Safety planning with follow-up reduces suicidal behaviors by approximately 50%;
problem: Stanley 2018 is a non-randomized cohort comparison (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.33-0.95; 3.03% vs 5.29%) that found SPI+ was 'associated with' 45% fewer suicidal behaviors; the card states a causal 50% reduction. Therapy on the Unit correctly says ~45%, associated, cohort not RCT.
whyItMatters: The standalone card teaches an RCT-grade causal effect size that learners will quote on rounds and exams, and it conflicts with the sibling page's calibrated statement.
evidence: Stanley B et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(9):894-900 (PMID 29998307): 'cohort comparison design'; 'SPI+ was associated with 45% fewer suicidal behaviors ... OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33-0.95'.
correction: Safety planning with follow-up was associated with ~45% fewer suicidal behaviors in a large VA ED cohort (Stanley 2018; not an RCT);

quote: **lowest cognitive demand → best inpatient fit** (Uphoff, *Cochrane* 2020)
problem: The inpatient-fit claim is attributed to Uphoff 2020, but that Cochrane review explicitly excluded RCTs conducted in inpatient settings; its BA-vs-TAU advantage was also moderate-certainty and not robust in worst-case/ITT sensitivity analyses.
whyItMatters: Learners will believe a Cochrane review established BA as the best inpatient intervention, when inpatient suitability is an extrapolation from outpatient trials.
evidence: Uphoff E et al. Behavioural activation therapy for depression in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;7:CD013305 (PMID 32628293, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD013305.pub2) — Selection criteria: 'We excluded RCTs conducted in inpatient settings'; BA vs TAU RR 1.40 (1.10-1.78), 'no longer evident in sensitivity analyses using a worst-case or intention-to-treat scenario'.
correction: (Uphoff, *Cochrane* 2020 — outpatient trials only; inpatient RCTs were excluded); **lowest cognitive demand → a reasonable inpatient fit by extrapolation**

quote: Repeat self-harm re-presentation 13.5% vs 22.1%, **NNT 12** (Hatcher 2011)
problem: Hatcher 2011 was null in its primary intention-to-treat analysis (13.4% vs 14.1% re-presentation, n=1,094); 13.5% vs 22.1% / NNT 12 is only the prespecified subgroup whose index episode was repeat self-harm, and the authors concluded PST 'is not recommended for everyone who presents to hospital with self-harm'.
whyItMatters: Presented without the subgroup qualifier, the cell teaches that a single Zelen RCT showed PST cuts re-presentation with NNT 12 across self-harm presentations, when the overall trial showed no effect.
evidence: Hatcher S et al. Br J Psychiatry 2011;199(4):310-316 (PMID 21816868, doi:10.1192/bjp.bp.110.090126): all episodes 13.4% vs 14.1%, P=0.79; first-episode 13.4% vs 9.4%; repeat-self-harm subgroup 13.5% vs 22.1%, NNT 12, P=0.03.
correction: In the prespecified subgroup presenting with *repeat* self-harm, re-presentation 13.5% vs 22.1%, **NNT 12**; no effect in the trial overall (Hatcher 2011)

quote: Safety Planning Intervention with follow-up ≈ **50% fewer suicidal behaviors** (Stanley 2018)
problem: Rounds the cohort-study estimate (45% fewer, OR 0.56) up to 50% and drops the observational design, inconsistent with Therapy on the Unit's '~45% ... a cohort comparison, not an RCT'.
whyItMatters: Minor overstatement of a non-randomized effect; learners see two different figures for the same study.
evidence: Stanley B et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(9):894-900 (PMID 29998307).
correction: Safety Planning Intervention with follow-up was associated with ≈ **45% fewer suicidal behaviors** (Stanley 2018, cohort comparison)

quote: A family member may bridge only in an emergency while an interpreter is being arranged, or at the patient's specific, documented request.
problem: Omits two limits of the federal rule: a minor child may interpret only in an emergency (never merely on request), and on request the accompanying adult must agree and reliance must be appropriate — which it rarely is for psychiatric risk assessment.
whyItMatters: A learner could accept a patient's child as interpreter, or use a relative to interpret a suicide or violence assessment, on the strength of a stated request.
evidence: Section 1557 ACA final rule, 45 CFR 92.201(e) (2024): accompanying adult only in an emergency involving imminent threat or on the individual's specific request with the adult's agreement where reliance is appropriate; minor children only in an emergency where no qualified interpreter is immediately available.
correction: A family member may bridge only in an emergency while an interpreter is being arranged, or at the patient's specific, documented request when the relative agrees and the topic allows it (never a minor child except in an emergency, and not for risk assessment).

quote: About 12–15% of psychiatric patients are readmitted within 30 days (20–25% for schizophrenia), and only ~50% receive a mental-health visit within 7 days.
problem: Three statistics with no source, on a page where every other number is attributed; the ~50% 7-day figure matches a single NY Medicaid sample (Haselden 2019: 53%) rather than a national rate, and readmission figures vary widely by payer and dataset.
whyItMatters: Learners will quote precise-looking national figures that cannot be traced or checked.
evidence: Haselden M et al. Psychiatr Serv 2019;70(10):860-866 (PMID 31310186) — 53% attended within 7 days in 179 NY Medicaid inpatients; national 30-day readmission and HEDIS FUH 7-day rates (NCQA; AHRQ HCUP) would settle the others.
correction: Roughly one in eight psychiatric inpatients is readmitted within 30 days (more with schizophrenia), and in many samples only about half attend a mental-health visit within 7 days (e.g., Haselden 2019, NY Medicaid: 53%).
verified: PubMed abstract PMID 31310186 for the 7-day figure; readmission figures by recall

quote: Firearms are involved in ~50% of US suicides
problem: Firearms have accounted for more than half of US suicides for years (~55% in 2022-2023 CDC mortality data); '~50%' understates it.
whyItMatters: Small, but it understates the single most important lethal-means target in US means-safety counselling.
evidence: CDC WISQARS / NCHS final mortality data 2022 (27,032 firearm suicides of 49,476, ~55%); 2023 similar.
correction: Firearms are involved in more than half (~55%) of US suicides

quote: **family/group-format psychoeducation was the standout for recurrence (OR 0.12, 0.02–0.94)**, and **family/conjoint therapy improved treatment retention (OR 0.46, 0.26–0.82)** and helped stabilize depressive symptoms (SMD −0.46, not significant)
problem: Mis-summarises Miklowitz 2021: OR 0.12 compares psychoeducation delivered in family/group format with the same strategies delivered individually (a component comparison, not vs control), retention OR 0.46 is vs standard psychoeducation, and 'helped stabilize ... not significant' is self-contradictory (95% CI −1.01 to 0.08 crosses zero; authors: 'with less certainty').
whyItMatters: Learners will believe family-format psychoeducation cuts bipolar recurrence ~8-fold vs usual care and that family therapy demonstrably improves depressive symptoms, neither of which the paper shows.
evidence: Miklowitz DJ et al. JAMA Psychiatry 2021;78(2):141-150 (PMID 33052390, doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2020.2993): 'Psychoeducation ... in a family or group format was associated with reducing recurrences vs the same strategies in an individual format (OR 0.12; 95% CI 0.02-0.94)'; family/conjoint therapy SMD −0.46 (−1.01 to 0.08) 'with less certainty'; retention OR 0.46 'compared with standard psychoeducation'.
correction: **psychoeducation delivered in a family or group format reduced recurrence relative to the same content delivered individually (OR 0.12, 0.02–0.94)**, and **family/conjoint therapy was associated with better retention than standard psychoeducation (OR 0.46, 0.26–0.82)**; its effect on depressive symptoms was uncertain (SMD −0.46, CI crossing zero)

quote: high-EE roughly **quintuples relapse odds (OR ~4.87)**
problem: OR 4.87 in Ma 2021 applies only to early relapse (≤12 months); for later relapse the OR was 2.13. Therapy on the Unit states this timing correctly; this page and its key-point card do not.
whyItMatters: Learners overgeneralise the five-fold figure to all relapse, and the two pages give different numbers for the same paper.
evidence: Ma CF et al. Psychol Med 2021;51(3):365-375 (PMID 33568244): early relapse (≤12 months) OR 4.87 (3.22-7.36); late relapse (>12 months) OR 2.13 (1.36-3.35); warmth OR 0.35.
correction: high-EE roughly **quintuples the odds of relapse within 12 months (OR ~4.87; ~2-fold for later relapse, OR 2.13)**

quote: the clinical work that changes outcomes is in Phase 3 (family perspective) and Phase 4 (shared planning), not the didactic.
problem: No study isolates which phase of a single family meeting changes outcomes; and the evidence base the library cites (family psychoeducation, Rodolico 2022; Xia 2011) is for structured illness education plus skills — so dismissing 'the didactic' contradicts Family Therapy Modalities, which calls psychoeducation the highest-evidence approach.
whyItMatters: A red-flag card teaches learners to deprioritise the structured illness education that carries the evidence, on the strength of an unsupported claim.
evidence: Rodolico A et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2022 (family psychoeducation alone OR 0.18 vs TAU); Xia 2011 Cochrane CD002831; no trial compares components of a single inpatient family meeting.
correction: the work families most often miss out on is in Phase 3 (family perspective) and Phase 4 (shared planning) — keep the didactic structured and brief so it does not crowd them out.

quote: an interpreter if needed
problem: Does not specify a qualified professional interpreter; in a family meeting the default risk is a bilingual relative interpreting, which the collateral page correctly prohibits.
whyItMatters: Learners may let a family member interpret the meeting, distorting both the patient's and the family's accounts and breaching confidentiality.
evidence: 45 CFR 92.201 (Section 1557); the library's own collateral_workflow.md rule.
correction: a qualified professional interpreter if anyone needs one (not a family member)

quote: This is the phase that most changes outcomes; protect the time for it.
problem: Asserted as established fact without evidence; no study attributes outcome change to a particular phase of a single family meeting (repeated in the key-points card).
whyItMatters: Learners take a teaching heuristic for an evidence-based finding.
evidence: Family-intervention evidence (Pharoah 2010; Rodolico 2022) concerns multi-session programmes, not phases of a single meeting.
correction: In our experience this is the phase most often squeezed out, and it is where expressed emotion becomes workable; protect the time for it.

quote: structured psychoeducation (readmission NNT ~5 in psychosis)
problem: The overlay card states readmission NNT ~5 without the caveat the page itself insists on (206 participants, 'hospital-based studies of limited quality', 'true size of effect is likely to be less'); overlay and prose disagree on how the number may be used.
whyItMatters: The card is what learners see first and quote; the page explicitly says 'don't quote NNT 5 as though it were precise'.
evidence: Xia J, Merinder LB, Belgamwar MR. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(6):CD002831 — readmission RR 0.71, NNT 5, n=206; authors' caveat on limited-quality hospital-based studies. The page's §2b quotes this caveat.
correction: structured psychoeducation (readmission NNT ~5 in psychosis, from 206 participants in limited-quality trials — likely an overestimate)
verified: recall; page's own quotation of Xia 2011

quote: You can always listen to a family without the patient's permission — consent governs what you share, not what you hear.
problem: 'Always listen' leaves out the caveat that acknowledging the admission, or placing an outbound call, discloses PHI. That needs the patient's agreement or a HIPAA exception.
whyItMatters: A learner acting on this card may call a relative, or confirm the admission to an inbound caller, to 'just listen', breaching HIPAA and the patient's trust — especially where the patient has objected to family contact.
evidence: HIPAA Privacy Rule 45 CFR 164.510(a)-(b) (facility directory opt-out; disclosures to family require agreement/opportunity to object except incapacity or emergency); HHS OCR guidance 'HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health' (2014, updated) — providers may listen to family concerns but should not confirm presence if the patient objected.
correction: You can listen to a family without the patient's permission — but without it (and absent a recognized exception such as incapacity or emergency) don't confirm the admission or share anything back; consent governs what you share, including that they are here, not what you hear.

verification.reason: HHS OCR guidance says HIPAA does not stop a provider from listening to family, but confirming that a patient is on a psychiatric unit, or phoning a relative, is itself a disclosure and needs agreement or a 164.510(b) exception. The reviewer's fix is right in substance but says flatly 'do not ... share anything back', which contradicts the incapacity/emergency exceptions; reworded so it matches M07-006.
verification.evidence: recall: 45 CFR 164.510(a)-(b), 164.512(j); HHS OCR 'HIPAA Privacy Rule and Sharing Information Related to Mental Health' FAQ (providers may listen to family concerns).

quote: psychoeducation carries the strongest single-intervention numbers in psychosis.
problem: Superlative unsupported: the NNT 5 rests on 206 participants in low-quality trials, and family intervention (Pharoah 2010, NNT 7 over 32 RCTs) and family psychoeducation (Rodolico 2022, OR 0.18) carry comparable or stronger evidence; the prior review's equivalent superlative was removed from Brief Psychotherapy.
whyItMatters: Learners carry an overconfident ranking of psychosocial interventions into exams and rounds.
evidence: Xia 2011 Cochrane CD002831; Pharoah 2010 Cochrane CD000088 (PMID 21154340); Rodolico 2022 Lancet Psychiatry.
correction: psychoeducation is among the best-supported psychological interventions in psychosis, though its headline NNTs rest on limited-quality trials.

quote: You can always *receive* information from a family — observations, history, concerns — without the patient's permission. Consent governs what you share, not what you hear.
problem: Same unqualified 'always': receiving information is permitted, but acknowledging the patient's presence on the unit, or initiating contact, discloses PHI and requires agreement or a HIPAA exception (incapacity, emergency, serious threat).
whyItMatters: Taught as a universal rule, it licenses outbound calls and presence-confirmation that breach confidentiality when the patient has declined family contact.
evidence: 45 CFR 164.510(a)-(b); 45 CFR 164.512(j); HHS OCR mental-health information-sharing guidance.
correction: You can always *receive* information from a family — observations, history, concerns — without the patient's permission, provided you do not confirm the patient is here or share anything back unless the patient agrees or a recognized exception (incapacity, emergency, serious threat) applies. Consent governs what you share, not what you hear.

verification.reason: The §6 family-meeting text has the same unqualified 'always' and nothing nearby qualifies it (the resident extension's 'consent-scope check' covers the meeting, not the call). The correction is accurate, keeps the teaching point, and reads grammatically in place.
verification.evidence: recall: 45 CFR 164.510(b)(1)-(3); 45 CFR 164.512(j); HHS OCR mental-health information-sharing guidance.

quote:
but discharge risk remains high because
> he refuses family collateral.
problem: The model presentation treats a patient's refusal to consent to collateral as a cause of higher risk. The refusal leaves an information gap and uncertainty. It is not in itself a risk factor, and it is the patient's right, subject to HIPAA's emergency exceptions.
whyItMatters: Learners would learn to frame refusal of consent as dangerousness, which can become punitive or coercive documentation in a note that carries legal weight.
evidence: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.510(b) and 164.512(j) (limits and emergency exceptions for family disclosure; receiving collateral does not itself require consent); general risk-formulation practice separating risk factors from missing data.
correction:
but discharge risk is still uncertain because
> he has not agreed to family collateral, so we lack baseline and home-safety data.

quote: **1. What are the DSM-5 Criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia?**
problem: Throughout the page (Q1, Q16, Q22, Q70, Q81, Q85 headings), criteria are attributed to "DSM-5" rather than the current DSM-5-TR (2022). The criteria content for these items is unchanged, so this is a currency label issue only.
whyItMatters: A nationally adopted curriculum should name the current edition, and learners should cite DSM-5-TR.
evidence: APA, DSM-5-TR (March 2022).
correction: **1. What are the DSM-5-TR Criterion A symptoms of schizophrenia?**

quote: All current antipsychotics modulate dopamine — most are D2 receptor antagonists or partial agonists.
problem: The sentence presents dopamine and D2 action as universal to antipsychotics, which pimavanserin and xanomeline–trospium contradict. The reviewer's correction named only one of these two exceptions.
whyItMatters: Learners would believe D2 blockade is a necessary property of every antipsychotic. They would miss the first mechanistically distinct schizophrenia agent, a current exam and rounds topic.
evidence: FDA approval of xanomeline–trospium chloride (Cobenfy) for adult schizophrenia, September 26, 2024. The label describes an M1/M4 muscarinic agonist mechanism without direct D2 antagonism.
correction: Nearly all current antipsychotics act directly at the D2 receptor, as antagonists or partial agonists. Exceptions include xanomeline–trospium (FDA-approved 2024 for schizophrenia), a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist with no direct D2 binding that is thought to modulate dopamine indirectly, and pimavanserin (a 5-HT2A inverse agonist approved for Parkinson's disease psychosis).

verification.reason: The finding is valid. Pimavanserin, a 5-HT2A inverse agonist approved for Parkinson's disease psychosis, has no dopaminergic action, and xanomeline–trospium (approved 2024-09-26) has no direct D2 binding, so 'all … modulate dopamine' and the implied D2-centred model are misleading. But xanomeline is thought to modulate dopamine indirectly, and the reviewer's 'The exception is xanomeline–trospium' is wrong because pimavanserin is a second exception. I corrected it to name both.

quote: Response in FEP is typically visible within **2 weeks** — if no improvement by then, reassess adherence and consider switching rather than waiting months.
problem: The pearl advises switching antipsychotics after 2 weeks without improvement in first-episode psychosis. Studies of first-episode patients specifically show that a substantial share respond later, and first-episode guidance calls for an adequate trial of about 4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose before switching. The 2-week early-non-improvement rule comes mainly from studies of multi-episode patients.
whyItMatters: Early switching can lead to cycling through agents, losing a drug that would have worked, and progressing prematurely toward a label of treatment resistance.
evidence: Emsley R et al., Am J Psychiatry 2006;163:743–745 (many first-episode responders respond after 4+ weeks). Gallego JA et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2011;72:1691–1696 (response accrues over months in first-episode schizophrenia). APA Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia, 3rd ed., 2020. Samara MT et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2015 (early non-improvement as a predictor, mostly in chronic samples).
correction: Early improvement is often visible within **2 weeks**, and its absence is a warning sign — check adherence and dose — but first-episode patients can respond late, so give an adequate trial (≥4–6 weeks at a therapeutic dose) before switching.

verification.reason: Q11 pearl stands alone with no FEP qualifier nearby. The primary FEP data contradict a 2-week switch rule: Emsley 2006 found 22.5% of FEP responders responded only after week 4 (11.2% after week 8), and Gallego 2011 found many FEP patients respond between weeks 8 and 16, with early limited improvement not a clinically useful predictor. The correction keeps the early-improvement signal and adds an adequate-trial floor.

problem: The current model of exposure therapy is inhibitory learning: violating the expectancy of harm and tolerating distress. The goal is not to wait until anxiety decreases within the session, and within-session habituation does not predict outcome.

correction: ERP works mainly through **inhibitory learning** — the patient confronts feared stimuli while resisting compulsions and learns that the feared outcome does not occur and that distress is tolerable; anxiety need not fall within the session.

correction: + diaphoresis → **serotonin syndrome** → stop serotonergic agents, supportive care + benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if moderate/persistent.

verification.reason: Management starts by stopping the serotonergic agents and giving supportive care plus benzodiazepines. Cyproheptadine is reserved for moderate cases that persist. The correction keeps the arrow format and the discriminators that precede the quote.

quote: Identifiable threatened victim → **duty to protect (Tarasoff)**.
problem: Presents the Tarasoff duty as universal. US states differ: some mandate a duty to warn or protect, some only permit disclosure, and a few impose no duty. The shelf page in this same chunk says the duty varies by jurisdiction.

quote: compounded by an **anticholinergic** started for BPH.*
problem: Standard BPH drugs (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors) are not anticholinergic; an antimuscarinic (e.g., oxybutynin) would be given for storage/urgency symptoms and is a hazard in BPH because it precipitates urinary retention — itself a delirium precipitant.
whyItMatters: Learners may think BPH treatment is anticholinergic and miss the teaching point that antimuscarinics in BPH risk retention.
evidence: AUA BPH/LUTS guideline (2021, amended 2023): antimuscarinics are add-on therapy for storage symptoms with low post-void residual; Beers Criteria (AGS 2023): avoid strongly anticholinergic drugs in older adults, especially with delirium or BPH/retention.
correction: compounded by an **anticholinergic** (e.g., oxybutynin) started for urinary symptoms — which in BPH also risks urinary retention.*

correction: **multicomponent non-pharmacologic strategies are the best-established interventions shown to reduce delirium incidence outside the ICU — by roughly 40–50%**
