quote: DBT remains the most evidence-based treatment, confirmed by multiple meta-analyses including a 2017 JAMA Psychiatry study.
problem: The 2017 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis (Cristea et al.) did not rank DBT above other therapies. It found DBT and psychodynamic approaches were the only types more effective than control, with small effects inflated by risk of bias and publication bias. The same deck's Q6 feedback says so correctly, so the two rationales contradict each other.
whyItMatters: The item misattributes a conclusion to a named paper and overstates the certainty of the evidence for DBT versus psychodynamic therapies.
evidence: Cristea IA et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2017;74:319-328 (PMID 28249086): DBT g=0.34, psychodynamic g=0.41, 'effects are small, inflated by risk of bias and publication bias'.
correction: DBT remains one of the best-studied treatments for BPD; a 2017 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis found DBT and psychodynamic approaches both more effective than control conditions, though with small effects.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: In the Bowden trial, which patient populations were identified as responding particularly well to divalproex compared to lithium?
problem: Bowden 1994 could not compare divalproex with lithium in rapid cycling: all eight patients with four or more manic episodes in the prior year were randomized to divalproex. The trial reported only that divalproex was as effective in rapid-cycling patients as in other patients. The mixed-state advantage over lithium comes from a later secondary analysis (Swann 1997).
whyItMatters: Learners and residents would cite a head-to-head subgroup superiority over lithium that the landmark trial never showed. That is a mis-summarised landmark result, taught as an answer key.
evidence: Bowden CL et al., JAMA 1994;271:918-24 (PMID 8120960), abstract: 'all eight patients with four or more manic episodes in the previous year were in the divalproex group ... Divalproex was as effective in rapid-cycling manic patients as in other patients.' Mixed or depressive mania: Swann AC et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1997 (secondary analysis).
correction: In the Bowden trial and its secondary analyses, divalproex was effective in which patient subgroups, in whom lithium has historically performed less well?

verification.reason: Bowden 1994 abstract confirms all eight rapid-cycling patients were randomised to divalproex, so no divalproex-vs-lithium subgroup comparison was possible; the trial says only that divalproex was as effective in rapid cyclers as in others. The mixed/depressive-mania signal is from the Swann 1997 secondary analysis. Downgraded to Moderate: it misattributes a trial result, but the clinical preference it teaches is still mainstream.
verification.evidence: Bowden CL et al., JAMA 1994;271:918-24 (PMID 8120960), abstract; Swann AC et al., Arch Gen Psychiatry 1997;54:37-42 (PMID 9006398)

sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: The trial was pivotal because it proved that divalproex was not inferior to lithium for acute stabilization.
problem: Bowden 1994 was a placebo-controlled superiority trial with a small lithium arm (n=35 in the ITT analysis, 2:1:2 allocation). It was not designed or powered to establish non-inferiority to lithium.
whyItMatters: It teaches a formal statistical claim (non-inferiority) that the trial did not test.
evidence: Bowden 1994 (PMID 8120960): 2:1:2 randomization; ITT n=68/35/73; both drugs superior to placebo.
correction: The trial was pivotal because both divalproex and lithium outperformed placebo with similar response rates, although it was not designed to formally test non-inferiority.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: Which of the following is considered a major absolute contraindication to the use of divalproex mentioned in the trial's clinical pearls?
problem: Under the US label, pregnancy is an absolute contraindication to valproate only for migraine prophylaxis. For bipolar disorder it carries a boxed warning: avoid unless other treatments have failed or are unacceptable. The label's absolute contraindications are hepatic disease, POLG mitochondrial disorders, urea cycle disorders and hypersensitivity.
whyItMatters: On an exam, learners would misidentify the label's absolute contraindications. The practical advice (avoid in pregnancy) is still sound.
evidence: Depakote (divalproex) US prescribing information: Contraindications (hepatic disease, POLG, urea cycle disorders, hypersensitivity, migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy); Boxed Warning (fetal risk).
correction: Which of the following is the most important reason to avoid divalproex, carried as a boxed warning and highlighted in the trial's clinical pearls?
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: The study confirmed that clozapine remains the most effective agent, standing alone in its superior efficacy compared to all other studied antipsychotics.
problem: Huhn 2019 ranked clozapine highest (SMD −0.89 vs placebo) but concluded that efficacy differences are 'gradual rather than discrete' with low or very low confidence. It excluded treatment-resistant patients, so it does not show clozapine significantly superior to every other agent.
whyItMatters: It overstates the paper and conflates acute multi-episode data with clozapine's established role in treatment resistance.
evidence: Huhn M et al., Lancet 2019;394:939-51 (PMID 31303314): TRS excluded; 'efficacy differences ... gradual rather than discrete'; confidence often low or very low.
correction: Clozapine had the largest effect size versus placebo (SMD −0.89), although the authors judged efficacy differences between drugs to be gradual rather than discrete, and treatment-resistant patients were excluded.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: Based on the study results, which drug demonstrates the highest efficacy but is limited by the worst side-effect profile (lowest acceptability)?
problem: The stem still says amitriptyline had the lowest acceptability, and the keyed feedback now contradicts it: clomipramine was the only agent worse than placebo for dropouts. In head-to-head trials amitriptyline was one of seven agents with the highest dropout rates, not the worst. The earlier fix (A3C1-F001) corrected only the feedback.
whyItMatters: The item contradicts itself, and a learner memorising the stem learns a false ranking.
evidence: Cipriani 2018 (PMID 29477251): clomipramine worse than placebo for acceptability (OR 1.30); amitriptyline, clomipramine, duloxetine, fluvoxamine, reboxetine, trazodone and venlafaxine had the highest dropout rates head-to-head.
correction: Based on the study results, which drug had the highest efficacy odds ratio but was among the agents with the highest dropout rates (poor acceptability)?
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: These two agents were specifically highlighted for providing the best overall balance between therapeutic effect and patient acceptability.
problem: The feedback says the 2018 NMA specifically highlighted escitalopram and sertraline as the best-balance pair. The paper names five agents with relatively higher response and lower dropout, and paroxetine and agomelatine are among them, so distractor A is also supported. The feedback misattributes the 2009 pairing, and the stem or distractor needs rewriting to leave one best answer. A feedback-only fix does not remove the ambiguity.
whyItMatters: Learners would attribute a 2009 finding to the 2018 paper and present it on rounds as the 2018 result. The distractor 'paroxetine and agomelatine' is also half-supported by the 2018 data, which leaves the item ambiguous.
evidence: Cipriani A et al., Lancet 2018;391:1357-66 (PMID 29477251), abstract: head-to-head, more effective were agomelatine, amitriptyline, escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, venlafaxine and vortioxetine; more tolerable were agomelatine, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, sertraline and vortioxetine. Cipriani A et al., Lancet 2009;373:746-58 (MANGA) identified sertraline and escitalopram as the best balance.
correction: Both appear among the five agents (escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, agomelatine and sertraline) that the 2018 analysis noted had relatively higher response and lower dropout; the escitalopram–sertraline pairing as the single best balance comes from Cipriani's earlier 2009 analysis of 12 antidepressants.

verification.reason: The finding's premise is partly wrong. The 2018 full text does name a balance group, in the sentence 'Some antidepressants, such as escitalopram, mirtazapine, paroxetine, agomelatine, and sertraline had a relatively higher response and lower dropout rate than the other antidepressants.' So escitalopram and sertraline are in it, but as two of five and not as a pair. That sentence also supports the distractor 'Paroxetine and agomelatine', so the item has two defensible answers. The escitalopram–sertraline pairing is from the 2009 MANGA analysis.
verification.evidence: Cipriani A et al., Lancet 2018;391:1357-66 (PMID 29477251, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32802-7), Europe PMC full text PMC5889788, Discussion; Cipriani A et al., Lancet 2009;373:746-58 (recall)

sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: The combination therapy yielded a 60% response rate, which was a modest but notable increase over either monotherapy alone.
problem: In Barlow 2000 the acute combined response (60.3% on the PDSS) was not significantly different from the other groups. Combination therapy's advantage appeared only by the end of maintenance, and after discontinuation the CBT+imipramine arm lost durability (26.3% vs 41.0% for CBT+placebo).
whyItMatters: Learners would believe combination therapy is acutely superior, which the trial did not show, and would miss that adding imipramine undermined CBT's durability.
evidence: Barlow DH et al., JAMA 2000;283:2529-36 (PMID 10815116): 'acute response rate for the combined treatment was 60.3% ... neither was significantly different from the other groups'; 6 months post-discontinuation CGI response 41.0% CBT+placebo vs 26.3% CBT+imipramine.
correction: The combination therapy yielded a numerically higher 60% response rate, but this was not statistically different from the other groups acutely; its advantage emerged during maintenance and was not durable after imipramine was stopped.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: Subsequent research (Tariot et al., 2004) confirmed that adding memantine to existing donepezil therapy provides additional benefit beyond monotherapy.
problem: 'Confirmed' overstates the evidence: DOMINO (Howard 2012) found no significant benefit of adding memantine to continued donepezil in moderate-to-severe AD, and meta-analytic add-on effects are small.
whyItMatters: Learners will tell families that combination therapy has proven additive benefit when the evidence is mixed and the effect modest.
evidence: Tariot PN et al., JAMA 2004;291:317-324 (benefit of adding memantine to stable donepezil); Howard R et al., NEJM 2012;366:893-903 (DOMINO: no significant benefit of donepezil plus memantine over donepezil alone).
correction: Tariot et al. (2004) found that adding memantine to stable donepezil gave modest additional benefit, although a later trial (DOMINO, 2012) did not find a significant benefit of the combination over donepezil alone.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: 'Rolling with resistance' to maintain engagement and the therapeutic alliance.
problem: 'Rolling with resistance' was retired in Motivational Interviewing (3rd ed., 2013) in favour of responding to sustain talk and discord, and Project MATCH did not test in-session resistance strategies, so the stem's 'recommended by the study's findings' is unsupported.
whyItMatters: Learners adopt superseded MI vocabulary and attribute an MI technique to a trial that did not examine it.
evidence: Miller WR, Rollnick S. Motivational Interviewing, 3rd ed. 2013 (and 4th ed. 2023): 'resistance' replaced by sustain talk and discord; Project MATCH Research Group, J Stud Alcohol 1997 (compared CBT, TSF, MET; no resistance-handling arm).
correction: Responding to sustain talk and discord without confrontation (formerly called 'rolling with resistance') to maintain engagement and the therapeutic alliance.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: What is a common overstatement or limitation to keep in mind when interpreting the results of the RAISE-ETP trial?
problem: Stem accepts either 'an overstatement' or 'a limitation'; the distractor 'benefits are uniform regardless of DUP' is, per its own feedback, 'a common overstatement', so two options satisfy the stem.
whyItMatters: A learner who correctly identifies the overstatement is marked wrong, teaching the opposite of the intended point.
evidence: Item's own distractor feedback: 'This is a common overstatement; the data showed that the benefits were significantly more pronounced in those with a shorter DUP.'
correction: Which limitation should you keep in mind when interpreting the results of the RAISE-ETP trial?
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: Re-key the item to match the deck's own overstatement-item convention (the key is the false claim): key 'The benefits of the program are uniform regardless of how long the patient was psychotic before treatment' as the common overstatement (its existing feedback already explains the DUP moderation), and reword the current keyed option into a true-statement distractor: 'The benefits were concentrated in patients with shorter duration of untreated psychosis (below the ~74-week median), so gains may be smaller when treatment starts late' — with feedback that this is an accurate limitation, not an overstatement: RAISE-ETP's moderator analysis showed greater benefit with shorter DUP, not that CSC is ineffective beyond 74 weeks.
problem: The keyed answer option is a pasted editorial remediation instruction, not an answer choice; the prior fix (A3C2-F003) was applied as literal text into the option slot, so learners see a paragraph of reviewer instructions marked 'keyed correct'.
whyItMatters: The item is unanswerable as shipped and exposes internal editorial text to learners; the stem remains double-keyed because the 'uniform benefit' distractor's feedback calls itself 'a common overstatement'.
evidence: Prior finding A3C2-F003 (2026-09-01) on this item; Kane JM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2016 (RAISE-ETP 2-year: benefit greater with DUP below the 74-week median). Note Robinson DG et al., Schizophr Bull 2022;48(5):1021-1031 (doi:10.1093/schbul/sbac053): at 5 years DUP did NOT moderate the QLS advantage (P=.32), so the DUP moderation is a 2-year finding.
correction: The 2-year benefits were concentrated in patients with shorter duration of untreated psychosis (below the 74-week median), so gains may be smaller when treatment starts late.
verified: PubMed: Robinson 2022 RAISE-ETP 5-year abstract; prior_findings A3C2-F003

verification.reason: The keyed option is a pasted editorial instruction. The replacement is accurate: DUP moderated benefit at 2 years (median 74 weeks), and Robinson 2022 found DUP did not moderate the QLS advantage at 5 years (P=.32), so the '2-year' qualifier is right. Because the stem reads 'overstatement or limitation', option 2 (whose feedback calls it 'a common overstatement') also qualifies as an answer. To end the double key, either change the stem to 'limitation' and make option 2's feedback say it is wrong, or re-key to option 2 as the prior finding proposed.
verification.evidence: Robinson DG et al., Schizophr Bull 2022;48:1021-31, PMID 35689478, doi:10.1093/schbul/sbac053; recall of Kane JM et al., Am J Psychiatry 2016 (DUP<74-week median moderation)

quote: This figure refers to the increase in suicide attempts in the general population after the warning was issued, not deaths within the trials.
problem: The 21.7% figure (Lu et al., BMJ 2014) is a relative rise in psychotropic-drug poisonings, used as a proxy for suicide attempts, among adolescents, not suicide attempts in the general population; the same study found no rise among adults and no change in completed suicides.
whyItMatters: Learners will misquote a contested observational proxy estimate as a population-wide rise in suicide attempts.
evidence: Lu CY et al., BMJ 2014;348:g3596 (doi:10.1136/bmj.g3596): psychotropic drug poisonings +21.7% (4.9-38.5%) adolescents, +33.7% young adults, +5.2% (NS) adults; completed suicides unchanged.
correction: This figure refers to a 21.7% relative rise in psychotropic-drug poisonings (a proxy for suicide attempts) among adolescents after the warning (Lu et al., BMJ 2014), not deaths within the trials.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: The benefits far outweigh the risks, with an NNT of 10 and an NNH of 143.
problem: Mixes denominators: NNT 10 is the MDD-specific figure, but NNH 143 is the pooled figure across all trials and indications (MDD, OCD, non-OCD anxiety). For MDD alone the suicidal ideation/attempt risk difference was 0.9% (NNH about 112) and not statistically significant, and Bridge described benefit as 'more modest in MDD'.
whyItMatters: Learners will quote an MDD benefit-risk ratio the paper did not report and overstate the margin ('far outweigh') for the indication where it was narrowest.
evidence: Bridge JA et al., JAMA 2007;297(15):1683-96 (doi:10.1001/jama.297.15.1683): MDD response RD 11.0% (NNT 10); SI/SA RD across all indications 0.7% (NNH 143); within MDD 0.9% (95% CI -0.1% to 1.9%), not significant.
correction: The benefits outweigh the risks: for MDD the NNT for response was 10, while the NNH for suicidal ideation/attempt pooled across all pediatric indications was 143 (the MDD-only increase was about 0.9% and not statistically significant).
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: The first 4–8 weeks of treatment.
problem: The FDA labelling asks for close monitoring during 'the initial few months' of therapy and at any dose change (increase or decrease); a 4-8 week window is narrower than the label and omits dose changes.
whyItMatters: A learner may relax suicidality monitoring after week 8 or after a dose increase, when the label still calls for close observation.
evidence: FDA class labelling for antidepressants, Boxed Warning and Warnings and Precautions 5.1 (Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors): monitor closely 'especially during the initial few months of drug therapy and at times of dosage changes'.
correction: The first few months of treatment and after any dose change.

verification.reason: The antidepressant class label says 'especially during the initial few months of drug therapy, and at times of dosage changes, either increases or decreases'. The 4-8 week figure echoes the 2004 visit schedule, which was later removed. Coordinator note: once dose changes are in the key, the 'tapering phase' distractor overlaps it, since a taper is a dose decrease. Its feedback ('the primary safety warning focuses on ... initiation') should be adjusted to say tapering is covered but is not the primary window.
verification.evidence: FDA antidepressant class labelling, Boxed Warning / W&P 5.1 (e.g., fluoxetine label on DailyMed, setid 32afb28a-dc4c-4a7e-9701-1825f805e7df); recall for wording.

sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: This meta-analysis synthesized data from 48 RCTs to provide the most robust evidence to date for lithium's effect on suicide and mortality.
problem: Presents Cipriani 2013 as the most robust evidence 'to date' without the later large placebo-controlled RCT (Katz 2022, VA, n=519) that found no reduction in repeat suicide-related events when lithium was added to usual care; the Cipriani suicide estimate (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03-0.66) rested on very few events.
whyItMatters: Learners will over-rely on adding lithium as a suicide-prevention intervention for a patient with a recent attempt, a use the only large dedicated RCT did not support.
evidence: Katz IR et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2022;79(1):24-32 (doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2021.3170): stopped for futility, HR 1.10 (0.77-1.55) for repeat suicide-related events; Cipriani A et al., BMJ 2013;346:f3646.
correction: This meta-analysis synthesized data from 48 RCTs, though its suicide estimate rested on few events; a later VA RCT (Katz et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2022; n=519) found that adding lithium to usual care after a recent suicide-related event did not reduce repeat events.
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: Lithium's anti-suicidal effect appears to be independent of its mood-stabilizing properties.
problem: Keyed as a 'clinical pearl from the study', but Cipriani 2013 did not test mechanism; independence from mood stabilization is a hypothesis (supported by some observational data), not a finding. The option's own feedback hedges to 'not fully explained'.
whyItMatters: Learners will state a speculative mechanism as an established fact on rounds and on exams.
evidence: Cipriani A et al., BMJ 2013;346:f3646 — discussion proposes reduced aggression/impulsivity as a possible mechanism; no mechanistic analysis was performed.
correction: Lithium's anti-suicidal effect may not be fully explained by its mood-stabilizing properties (a hypothesis, not something this meta-analysis tested).
sourceFile: audio-companion quiz deck data (see A3 transcript)

quote: There were no significant differences in efficacy between these structured psychotherapies.
problem: In the primary analysis CBT was statistically significantly (though trivially, g=0.06) more effective than other psychotherapies pooled; the difference lost significance in most sensitivity analyses. The paper did not report separate CBT-vs-IPT or CBT-vs-psychodynamic comparisons as the stem implies.
whyItMatters: Learners misreport the paper's result; the defensible teaching point is 'small and not robust', not 'no significant difference'.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: CBT's advantage over other psychotherapies was very small (g=0.06) and was not robust across sensitivity analyses.

quote: Combined treatment is superior to either pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy alone.
problem: Mis-keyed: the cited meta-analysis found combined treatment superior to pharmacotherapy alone but NOT more effective than CBT alone at short or long term.
whyItMatters: Learners would state on rounds and exams that the paper showed combination beats psychotherapy, the opposite of its finding.
evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15 (doi:10.1002/wps.21069): 'Combined treatment was more effective than pharmacotherapies alone ... but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'; 'CBT was significantly more effective than other psychotherapies, but the difference was small (g=0.06) and became non-significant in most sensitivity analyses.'
correction: Combined treatment is superior to pharmacotherapy alone but was not significantly more effective than CBT alone.

verification.reason: Checked against the PubMed abstract: combined treatment beat pharmacotherapy alone (g=0.51 short-term, 0.32 long-term) 'but it was not more effective than CBT alone at either time point'. The keyed option is wrong and the correction matches the paper. Sibling text keeps the error and must change in the same edit: option 4's feedback ('superior to both'), option 2's feedback, and Q6 option 1 ('combined > psychotherapy alone ... key finding'), which contradicts the new key.
verification.evidence: Cuijpers P et al., World Psychiatry 2023;22:105-15, PMID 36640411, doi:10.1002/wps.21069

quote: The meta-analysis confirmed that the synergy of medication and therapy provides better outcomes than either treatment modality used in isolation.
problem: Rationale inverts the finding for CBT alone.

correction: The meta-analysis found combined treatment more effective than pharmacotherapy alone at short and longer-term follow-up, but not more effective than CBT alone.

quote: Observing that combined treatment is more effective than psychotherapy alone.

quote: Rewrite the item to the review's actual result, e.g. stem: 'A 2022 Cochrane review of 15 RCTs evaluated Shared Decision-Making (SDM) interventions in mental health care. Which outcome showed some evidence of improvement?' keyed to 'Patients' perceived involvement in the decision-making process immediately after the encounter', with feedback that effects on knowledge, overall satisfaction, and clinical outcomes were uncertain (low- to very-low-certainty evidence). Align Q6's feedback with the same summary, and attribute knowledge/decisional-conflict gains to the general patient decision-aid literature if that teaching point is kept.
problem: The prior review's remediation instruction (A3C2-F007 'replacement') was pasted verbatim into the learner-facing stem; the options, key and feedback were never rewritten, so the item still keys 'Patient satisfaction and knowledge' while its own stem says that finding is uncertain.

quote: > Lethal means assessment reduced the risk of a suicide attempt or death within 180 days from 3.3 to 0.83%.
problem: The claim stands alone as a causal fact: roughly a 75% relative reduction. It leaves out that this is a quasi-experimental observational analysis (an instrumental-variable design on EHR data) in patients who endorsed suicidal ideation on the PHQ-9. The authors themselves warn that unmeasured co-occurring prevention practices may contribute to the effect.
whyItMatters: Learners and residents may quote 'asking about means cuts suicide attempts by three-quarters' as a trial result. That overstates certainty in exactly the lethal-means teaching this surface (exp_family) supports. The direction of the finding is right, but the size and the causal wording are not licensed.
evidence: Boggs JM et al., J Gen Intern Med 2020;35(6):1709-1714 (PMID 32040838). The title reads 'A Quasi-Experimental Analysis…'. Setting: Kaiser Permanente Colorado adults with suicidal ideation on the PHQ-9, 2010–2016. Limitations: 'Unmeasured suicide prevention practices that co-occur with lethal means assessment may contribute to the effects observed.'
correction: > In a quasi-experimental analysis of patients with suicide ideation reported on the PHQ-9, lethal means assessment reduced the risk of a suicide attempt or death within 180 days from 3.3 to 0.83% — an observational estimate, not a randomized trial result.
verified: PubMed abstract, PMID 32040838. Optionally extend the stored span to include the authors' limitations sentence.

whyItMatters: The 77% is quoted as if it were a trial response rate. The number is right, but learners should know it rests on case series and has no controlled comparator. The authors call for controlled studies.
evidence: Bot L et al., Acta Psychiatr Scand 2026;154(2):99-115 (PMID 42009596). The abstract says: 'Most were case series using lorazepam'; 'the need for… well-designed controlled studies'.
correction: Across 53 studies, mostly case series using lorazepam, benzodiazepine treatment of catatonia was associated with an overall response rate of 77%

quote: while severity of depression and suicidal ideation decreased comparably in both groups and outcomes were comparable between the two groups at 12-month follow-up.

whyItMatters: A resident reading the claim alone would think DBT matched or beat SSRI management on every outcome. They might then treat an SSRI as dispensable in a patient with BPD and comorbid major depression, when the trial showed a lower MDD rate on the SSRI.

quote: haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV/IM (or low-dose SGA), reassess q30–60 min, cumulative-dose cap and EPS/QTc vigilance [2].
problem: Patient A's plan gives haloperidol with no warning about antipsychotic sensitivity in Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia and no note that IV haloperidol is off-label and needs ECG monitoring.
whyItMatters: Haloperidol in DLB/PD can cause severe rigidity, immobility, NMS-like reactions and death; residents should screen for parkinsonism/DLB features before choosing the agent.
evidence: McKeith IG et al., DLB Consortium 4th consensus, Neurology 2017; AGS Beers Criteria 2023; FDA 2007 information for healthcare professionals on IV haloperidol (QT prolongation/TdP; not approved IV).
correction: haloperidol 0.5–1 mg IV/IM (or low-dose SGA), reassess q30–60 min, cumulative-dose cap and EPS/QTc vigilance [2] (IV haloperidol is off-label — ECG monitoring); avoid haloperidol if Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia is known or suspected (baseline parkinsonism or pre-existing hallucinations/fluctuations) — very-low-dose oral quetiapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable.

verification.reason: The DLB/PD sensitivity warning and the IV-haloperidol off-label/QT point are both valid. FDA's 2007 alert says IV haloperidol is not approved and recommends ECG monitoring if it is given IV. Quetiapine is oral-only, so the correction now says so; that matters for an agitated patient who may refuse oral medication. The DLB cue is phrased as a baseline feature to match S1-003.
verification.evidence: McKeith IG et al., Neurology 2017 (DLB 4th consensus); AGS Beers Criteria 2023; FDA Information for Healthcare Professionals: Haloperidol (2007) — recall.

quote: Meta-analysis of ED/prehospital data shows dissociative-dose ketamine (typically 4–5 mg/kg IM) achieves adequate sedation in roughly 5 minutes — faster than antipsychotic/benzodiazepine comparators
problem: Sullivan et al. 2020 [6] pooled sedation success (85%) and airway management (20%) and found no significant difference vs controls (sedation RR 1.95, 95% CI 0.47–8.1); it did not report a ~5-minute onset or show ketamine faster than comparators — those data come from individual studies (e.g., Cole 2016 prehospital ketamine vs haloperidol).
whyItMatters: Residents appraising evidence (as the facilitator notes require) are taught a meta-analytic conclusion the paper does not reach and miss its headline safety number (~20% airway management).
evidence: Sullivan N et al., Am J Emerg Med 2020;38(3):655–661, PMID 31902698 abstract: 13 studies; sedation 85%; airway management 20%; comparisons with controls not significant. Cole JB et al., Clin Toxicol 2016 (prehospital ketamine vs haloperidol, median ~5 vs ~17 min).
correction: Meta-analysis of ED/prehospital data shows dissociative-dose ketamine (typically 4–5 mg/kg IM) sedates ~85% of agitated patients, with airway management in ~20% and no statistically significant difference from comparators; individual prehospital studies report onset in roughly 5 minutes, faster than haloperidol

whyItMatters: Mis-attributes findings; the hypoactive-miss claim is true but rests on other work (e.g., Han 2009), so residents citing [10] would misrepresent it.
evidence: Schonnop R et al., CJEM 2022;24(8):820–831, PMID 36138324 abstract (four themes as listed).
correction: qualitative work attributes misses to inconsistent screening-tool use, assessment perceived as time-consuming and low priority, and unclear ownership of delirium recognition [10]; hypoactive presentations and attribution to dementia or "baseline" are classic miss patterns
